frames.narration: The first version of the duplicate check compares every pair of order ids. On a test list of n = 10 ids that is 45 comparisons, over before anyone notices.
At n = 1,000 the same code makes 499,500 comparisons. At an assumed one nanosecond per step that is half a millisecond, so nobody has a reason to look at it.
Ten times the data is not ten times the work. At n = 100,000 it is 4,999,950,000 steps, about 5 seconds: slow, but it finishes, and it is the size where a review comment would have mattered.
A year later a batch job feeds it 5,000,000 ids. That is about 12.5 trillion steps, over 3 hours of the machine doing nothing else. The size grew 50 times; the cost grew 2,500 times.
The developer reads the code for its shape: a loop inside a loop over the same list. That is O(n²), and the fix is to remember the ids already seen in a set: one pass, about n steps.
At n = 5,000,000 the set version takes about 5 million steps, a few milliseconds. The class changed from O(n²) to O(n), and that is a factor of 2.5 million at this size.

Now suppose each set operation costs 100 steps of hashing and memory traffic. At n = 50 the old pair check does 1,225 steps and the new one 5,000: the better class loses at small n. Constants are real, and Big O only says who wins for large n.
